question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words..
A speech made without preparation
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Extempore.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Extempore" means a speech, performance, or piece of writing that is done or composed without any preparation beforehand. (बिना पूर्व तैयारी के दिया गया भाषण)
◦ Example: The chief guest was asked to speak extempore, and he delivered a brilliant unscripted address.

• The word comes from the Latin "ex tempore", literally meaning "out of the time", i.e., something done on the spur of the moment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Parable (दृष्टान्त कथा): A simple story used to illustrate a moral or spiritual lesson.

• Option 2: Eulogy (प्रशंसा भाषण): A speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly, typically a tribute to someone who has died.

• Option 4: Chronicle (इतिवृत्त): A factual written account of important events in the order in which they happened.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutes often asked alongside "Extempore": Impromptu (done without being planned, used for actions in general, not just speeches), Verbatim (word for word), Eloquent (fluent and persuasive in speech).

• Do not confuse "Extempore" (a speech given without preparation) with "Extemporaneous", the adjective form used to describe such a speech.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Your ear has three main ______: outer, middle and inner.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. parts.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence lists three components of the ear — outer, middle and inner — so the blank must be filled with a word meaning divisions or components of a whole, which is exactly what "parts" means.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: In such vocabulary-based cloze sentences, the word chosen must fit both the grammatical structure (a plural countable noun after "main") and the logical meaning of the sentence (here, the three named items must be the sub-divisions of the ear).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "subjects" is incorrect because the outer, middle and inner ear are not academic subjects; the word does not fit the anatomical context.

• Option 3: "plugs" is incorrect because "ear plugs" are objects inserted into the ear, not divisions of the ear itself.

• Option 4: "events" is incorrect because "outer, middle and inner" cannot logically describe events; they describe physical regions.

NOTE

• The human ear is anatomically divided into three parts: the outer ear (pinna and ear canal), the middle ear (eardrum and ossicles), and the inner ear (cochlea and semicircular canals) — a common general-knowledge fact tested alongside vocabulary in such questions.

• In SSC cloze/blank questions, always read the full sentence first to identify the logical category the missing word belongs to, then eliminate options that do not match that category.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
Lee said to his wife, "I am very happy today."
option_1: Lee told his wife that he was very happy today.
option_2: Lee told his wife that he has been very happy that day.
option_3: Lee told his wife he was very happy today.
option_4: Lee told his wife that he was very happy that day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Lee told his wife that he was very happy that day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is in Direct Speech, with the reporting verb "said to" and the reported speech in the Simple Present Tense ("I am very happy today").

• Rule — Narration change (Assertive sentence, Present to Past):
◦ "said to" changes to "told" in the reporting verb.
◦ A conjunction "that" is added before the reported speech.
◦ The tense of the reported speech shifts one step back: "am" (Simple Present) becomes "was" (Simple Past).
◦ The pronoun "I" changes to agree with the subject of the reporting verb, becoming "he".
◦ The time expression "today" changes to "that day", since the speech is no longer being reported on the same day.

• Applying the rule: "I am very happy today" becomes "he was very happy that day", giving the full sentence: Lee told his wife that he was very happy that day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it keeps "today" instead of changing it to "that day", which is required when narration shifts from direct to indirect speech.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it changes the tense to "has been" (Present Perfect) instead of the correct "was" (Simple Past), and it also fails to change "today" to "that day".

• Option 3 is incorrect because although it omits the optional conjunction "that", it crucially keeps "today" unchanged, which is a definite error in narration.

NOTE

• Common time-expression changes in narration: today → that day; tomorrow → the next/following day; yesterday → the previous day/the day before; now → then; here → there; this → that; these → those; ago → before.

• If the reported speech expresses a universal truth or habitual fact, the tense is NOT changed even in indirect speech.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. bendable electronics and sensing technologies research
Q. people using "aerohaptics", creating feelings of touch with jets of air
R. my colleagues and I working in the University of Glasgow's
S. group have now developed a system of holograms of
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. RPSQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• To rearrange jumbled sentence parts, identify the part that can logically begin the sentence (usually containing the subject) and then trace the chain of ideas to the end.

• R — "my colleagues and I working in the University of Glasgow's" — introduces the subject ("my colleagues and I") and naturally opens the sentence.

• P — "bendable electronics and sensing technologies research" — follows R, completing the phrase "the University of Glasgow's bendable electronics and sensing technologies research...".

• S — "group have now developed a system of holograms of" — follows P, completing "...research group have now developed a system of holograms of..." and supplying the main verb "have developed".

• Q — "people using "aerohaptics", creating feelings of touch with jets of air" — logically ends the sentence, explaining what the system of holograms consists of.

• Joining them: "My colleagues and I working in the University of Glasgow's bendable electronics and sensing technologies research group have now developed a system of holograms of people using "aerohaptics", creating feelings of touch with jets of air." This gives the order R-P-S-Q.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: QPSR is incorrect because it begins with Q, which refers back to "people using aerohaptics" — a phrase with no clear subject of its own to open the sentence.

• Option 3: PQRS is incorrect because it places P ("bendable electronics...") first, but this phrase is a continuation of "University of Glasgow's" from R and cannot stand as an opening.

• Option 4: SRQP is incorrect because it opens with S ("group have now developed..."), which requires a preceding noun ("research group") to make grammatical sense, breaking the logical flow.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always look first for the part containing the subject and finite main verb, and note connecting words/pronouns that hint at sequence (e.g., "of" at the end of S needs an object, which only Q supplies).

• Possessive markers like "Glasgow's" at the end of one part are strong clues that a noun phrase (like "research group") must follow immediately.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Burnig.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Burning" (present participle of "burn"), not "Burnig".

• Rule: "Burnig" is missing the letter "n" before the suffix "-ing" — the correct formation is the full root "burn" + "-ing" = "burning".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Morning" is correctly spelt — it refers to the early part of the day.

• Option 2: "Washing" is correctly spelt — the present participle/gerund of "wash".

• Option 3: "Calling" is correctly spelt — the present participle/gerund of "call".

NOTE

• When adding "-ing" to a verb ending in a single consonant preceded by a single stressed vowel (like "run" → "running"), the final consonant is doubled; "burn" ends in two consonants ("rn"), so no doubling occurs — it simply becomes "burning".

• Commonly confused "-ing" spellings tested by SSC: beginning (double n), occurring (double r), travelling, writing (drop silent e).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Its impossible to conduct truly causal research on media consumption and suicide.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Its impossible to conduct.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Its" used here is the possessive adjective (meaning "belonging to it"), but the sentence requires the contraction "It's", short for "It is".

• Rule: "It's" (with an apostrophe) is always the contracted form of "it is" or "it has"; "Its" (without an apostrophe) is the possessive form used before a noun (e.g., "the dog wagged its tail"). Since the sentence means "It is impossible to conduct...", an apostrophe is required.

• Corrected sentence: "It's impossible to conduct truly causal research on media consumption and suicide."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "media consumption and suicide." is grammatically correct as written; it contains no error.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, in the segment "Its impossible to conduct".

• Option 4: "truly causal research on" is grammatically correct; "truly" correctly modifies the adjective "causal".

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophones tested by SSC: its/it's, their/there/they're, your/you're, whose/who's.

• Memory tip: if you can expand the word to "it is" or "it has" and the sentence still makes sense, use "it's"; otherwise use "its".

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
Exaggerated claims, not meant to be taken seriously
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Hyperbole.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Hyperbole" means a deliberate exaggeration used for effect, not meant to be taken literally. (अतिशयोक्ति)
◦ Example: "I've told you a million times" is a hyperbole, not a literal claim.

• The word comes from the Greek "hyper" (beyond) + "ballein" (to throw), i.e., to throw or go beyond the literal truth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Hyperpyrexia (अतितीव्र ज्वर): A medical term for an extremely high fever.

• Option 3: Hypergamy (उच्चतर वर्ग में विवाह): The practice of marrying a person of a higher social or economic class.

• Option 4: Hyperreal (अतियथार्थ): Having a more vivid or detailed quality than reality itself, often used in art/media theory.

NOTE

• Other "hyper-" prefix words tested by SSC: hyperactive (excessively active), hypersensitive (overly sensitive), hypertension (high blood pressure), hyperbolic (adjective form of hyperbole, exaggerated).

• Do not confuse "Hyperbole" with "Understatement", its opposite figure of speech, where something is deliberately presented as less significant than it is.

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
The child locked the shutters.
option_1: The shutters were locked by the child.
option_2: The shutters are locked by the child.
option_3: The shutters would be locked by the child.
option_4: The shutters had been locked by the child.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The shutters were locked by the child.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The child locked the shutters" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the shutters" (plural) becomes the subject, so the auxiliary is "were"; the verb "locked" becomes the past participle "locked" (V3, same form for regular verbs); and "the child" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The shutters were locked by the child.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "are locked" is the passive form of the Simple Present Tense, not the Simple Past Tense used in the active sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "would be locked" introduces the modal "would", changing the meaning and tense entirely; it is not present in the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "had been locked" is the passive of the Past Perfect Tense, which requires a different context (an action completed before another past action).

NOTE

• The passive of the Simple Past Tense always uses "was" (singular subject) or "were" (plural subject) + the past participle (V3).

• Regular verbs like "lock" have the same form for V2 and V3 (locked/locked), so students must rely on the auxiliary verb, not the main verb, to identify the tense in such questions.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
What is the price of this fancy dress pink?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. fancy dress pink?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the order of adjectives before the noun "dress". When a descriptive/type adjective and a colour adjective both modify a noun, standard English places the colour adjective closer to the noun.

• Rule — Order of adjectives: Determiner → Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Colour → Origin → Material → Purpose/Type + Noun. Here, "fancy" is a descriptive/type adjective and "pink" is a colour adjective, so "pink" must come immediately before "dress".

• Corrected sentence: "What is the price of this pink fancy dress?"

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "No error" is incorrect because the segment "fancy dress pink" does contain a word-order error.

• Option 3: "price of this" is grammatically correct as written; it contains no error.

• Option 4: "What is the" is grammatically correct; it is a standard question-opening structure.

NOTE

• SSC frequently tests adjective order errors — remember the acronym OSASCOMP: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose.

• Example of correct order: "a beautiful small old round red Indian wooden carving box".

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
As hard as nails
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Physically or mentally tough.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "As hard as nails" means extremely tough, either physically (showing no sign of pain or weakness) or mentally/emotionally (showing no sympathy or sentiment). (शारीरिक या मानसिक रूप से बहुत कठोर/मज़बूत)
◦ Example: After years in the army, he became as hard as nails and never complained about the harsh conditions.

• The comparison is to the physical hardness of iron nails, extended metaphorically to describe a person's resilience or lack of emotion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To be stubborn" describes unwillingness to change one's opinion, a different idea (usually expressed by idioms like "as stubborn as a mule").

• Option 2: "To feel no pain" captures only part of the physical sense and misses the mental-toughness aspect entirely.

• Option 4: "Hard working" relates to diligence and effort, unrelated to the idiom's meaning of toughness or resilience.

NOTE

• Other "hard" idioms tested by SSC: "Hard nut to crack" (a difficult problem or person), "Hard and fast rule" (a rule that cannot be changed), "Learn the hard way" (to learn through difficult experience).

• Compare with "as soft as butter", an idiom with the opposite meaning of being gentle or easily influenced.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. These components can work independently.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spellings required are "components" (parts of a whole) and "independently" (without being influenced by others) — both spelt correctly only in Option 3.

• Rule: "Component" is spelt com-po-nent (not "componant"), and "independently" is spelt in-de-pend-ent-ly (not "indepedently", and with the root verb "work" spelt correctly, not "wrok").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "componants" is incorrect; the correct ending is "-ents", not "-ants".

• Option 2: "indepedently" is incorrect; it is missing the letter "n" (should be "independently").

• Option 4: "wrok" is incorrect; the letters are transposed — the correct spelling is "work".

NOTE

• Words ending in "-ent/-ents" vs "-ant/-ants" are a common SSC trap: e.g., component, resident, president, different (all "-ent") versus assistant, servant, tenant (all "-ant") — there is no fixed rule, so these must be memorised.

• Always read silently letter-by-letter when a word looks "almost right", since transposition errors (like wrok/work) are easy to miss at a glance.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
The number of women working outside homes has been steady increasing.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. has been steadily.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the sentence, the underlined phrase "has been steady" is followed by the present participle "increasing", which is a verb form and must be modified by an adverb, not an adjective.

• Rule: Adjectives (like "steady") modify nouns, while adverbs (like "steadily") modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Since "increasing" is a verb (part of the present perfect continuous structure "has been increasing"), it needs the adverb "steadily" to describe how the number is increasing.

• Corrected sentence: "The number of women working outside homes has been steadily increasing."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "had been steadier" is incorrect because "steadier" is a comparative adjective, not an adverb, and "had been" (Past Perfect Continuous) does not fit the ongoing present context of the sentence.

• Option 3: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence contains a clear error — an adjective is wrongly used where an adverb is required.

• Option 4: "have been steady" is incorrect both because "steady" remains an adjective (not an adverb) and because "have been" does not agree with the singular subject "The number".

NOTE

• Common adjective-to-adverb pairs tested by SSC: steady → steadily, quick → quickly, careful → carefully, rapid → rapidly.

• Remember: the subject "The number of women..." takes a singular verb ("has"), since "The number" (not "women") is the head noun of the subject.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
The ______ heard that the relationship was stormy and had broken up several times.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. inquiry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence needs a noun that can be the subject of "heard", referring to a formal investigative body or process, which is exactly what "inquiry" (also spelt "enquiry") means.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: The blank must be filled by a noun that fits the sentence structure as the subject of "heard"; this immediately favours "inquiry" over the other options, which are not matching nouns in this sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "impute" is a verb meaning to attribute or credit a fault to someone; it cannot function as the subject noun of the sentence.

• Option 3: "inordinate" is an adjective meaning excessive or unrestrained; it cannot stand alone as a noun subject.

• Option 4: "impugn" is a verb meaning to challenge or dispute the truth of something; like "impute", it cannot serve as the sentence's subject noun.

NOTE

• Be careful to distinguish parts of speech in fill-in-the-blank questions: the blank here needs a noun, which immediately eliminates any verb or adjective options regardless of their meaning.

• Commonly confused words: inquiry/enquiry (an investigation or a question), impute vs impugn (to attribute a fault to someone vs to challenge the truth of something).

question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below.
Fret
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Relax.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Fret" means to be constantly worried or anxious about something. (चिंतित होना/कुढ़ना)
◦ Example: There's no need to fret over the exam results; you did your best.

• Its antonym must express the opposite state — being calm and free of worry, which is exactly what "Relax" means. (शांत होना/तनावमुक्त होना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Anxious (चिंतित): A near-synonym of "fret", not its opposite — both describe a state of worry.

• Option 2: Anguish (पीड़ा/व्यथा): Severe mental or physical pain or suffering; again a synonym in feeling, not an antonym.

• Option 4: Pine (तड़पना): To long for something or someone with sadness; related in tone to "fret" rather than opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "fret": worry, agonize, brood, fuss.

• Other antonyms of "fret"/"worry" tested by SSC: calm down, be at ease, be composed, unwind.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
The whys and wherefores
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Reasons.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "The whys and wherefores" means the reasons or explanations for something; the full details of why something happened. (किसी बात के सारे कारण/स्पष्टीकरण)
◦ Example: The manager did not go into the whys and wherefores of the decision; he simply announced it.

• The phrase pairs two old-fashioned question words — "why" (for what reason) and "wherefore" (for what purpose) — to emphasise a complete explanation of causes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: References (संदर्भ): Sources cited or mentioned, unrelated to giving reasons for an action.

• Option 2: Circumstances (परिस्थितियाँ): The conditions or facts surrounding an event — related but not identical to "reasons" for it.

• Option 3: Requirements (आवश्यकताएँ): Things that are needed, a different concept from explaining causes.

NOTE

• The phrase famously echoes Shakespeare's "Romeo and Juliet": "wherefore art thou Romeo" — where "wherefore" means "why", not "where".

• Similar idioms of explanation: "the ins and outs" (all the details of a situation), "the nitty-gritty" (the most important practical details).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Enigmatic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Mysterious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Enigmatic" means difficult to understand or interpret; mysterious and puzzling. (रहस्यमय/समझ में न आने वाला)
◦ Example: She gave an enigmatic smile that revealed nothing about her true feelings.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Mysterious", which shares the same core sense of being puzzling or hard to explain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Literate (साक्षर): Able to read and write — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 2: Grumpy (चिड़चिड़ा): Bad-tempered or irritable — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: Illiterate (अनपढ़): Unable to read and write; roughly opposite in sense to "literate", and unrelated to "enigmatic".

NOTE

• The noun form is "enigma" (a person or thing that is mysterious or difficult to understand).

• Other synonyms of "enigmatic": cryptic, inscrutable, puzzling, baffling.

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
Decimate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. wreck.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Decimate" means to destroy or kill a large proportion of something; to severely damage or ruin. (बड़े पैमाने पर नष्ट करना)
◦ Example: The forest fire decimated the wildlife population in the region.

• Among the given options, "wreck" (to destroy or ruin something completely) is closest in meaning to this sense of severe destruction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: mend (मरम्मत करना): To repair or fix something — nearly opposite in meaning to "decimate".

• Option 3: harbour (शरण देना): To keep or hold a thought/feeling, or to give shelter; unrelated to destruction.

• Option 4: establish (स्थापित करना): To set up or found something permanently — opposite in sense to destroying.

NOTE

• Originally, "decimate" meant to kill one in every ten (from Latin "decimus", tenth) — a punishment used in the Roman army — but in modern usage it broadly means to destroy a large part of something.

• Other synonyms of "decimate": devastate, ravage, annihilate, demolish.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
The humour of the gods is cruel; or ______ they see more than we do.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. perhaps.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence presents two possible explanations joined by "or": that the gods' humour is cruel, or — introducing a tentative alternative possibility — that they simply "see more than we do". This tentative, speculative sense is expressed by the adverb "perhaps" (meaning "possibly").

• Rule — Contextual word choice: The blank must logically connect an alternative possibility to the first clause; "perhaps" fits both grammatically (as a sentence adverb) and semantically (expressing a possibility, not a certainty or contrast).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "unlikely" is incorrect because it expresses doubt about something happening, which does not logically fit as an alternative explanation here.

• Option 2: "odds" is a noun (as in "the odds are") and cannot grammatically fit directly before "they see" in this construction.

• Option 4: "however" is incorrect because it signals a contrast, but the sentence is offering an alternative possible reason, not contradicting the first clause.

NOTE

• Adverbs of possibility commonly tested by SSC: perhaps, maybe, possibly, probably — each can introduce an alternative or tentative idea within a sentence.

• "However" is a conjunctive adverb of contrast, typically used to introduce a statement that opposes the previous one, unlike "perhaps", which expresses uncertainty.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
I didn't have times to watch the whole movie.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. time to watch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase uses "times", the plural form of the countable noun "time" (an occasion), but the sentence requires "time" used as an uncountable noun meaning available duration/opportunity to do something.

• Rule: When "time" refers to a quantity or duration (as in "I don't have time to do something"), it is uncountable and never takes a plural "-s" or the indefinite article "a". It only becomes countable ("times") when referring to occasions or instances (e.g., "three times a day").

• Corrected sentence: "I didn't have time to watch the whole movie."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "timer to watched" is incorrect because "timer" (a device) is the wrong word entirely, and "to watched" is an incorrect infinitive form ("to" must be followed by the base form of the verb).

• Option 3: "time to watching" is incorrect because "to" here is part of the infinitive "to watch" (expressing purpose), not a preposition, so it must be followed by the base verb, not the "-ing" form.

• Option 4: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain an error — the uncountable noun "time" was wrongly pluralised.

NOTE

• "Time" as an uncountable noun: "I have no time", "save time", "spend time" — never pluralised in these senses.

• "Time" as a countable noun (occasions): "three times", "several times", "this time" — pluralised freely in this sense.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Oblate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Mendicant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Oblate" (as a noun) refers to a person who has dedicated themselves to a religious life, especially one living by vows within or attached to a monastic community. (धार्मिक जीवन हेतु समर्पित व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: He became an oblate of the Benedictine monastery in his later years, devoting himself to prayer and service.

• Among the given options, "Mendicant" — a member of a religious order who lives a life of dedication and simplicity, traditionally supported through alms — is closest in sense to a person devoted to religious/monastic life.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Heathen (अधर्मी): A person who does not belong to a widely-held religion, historically used for non-believers — nearly opposite to someone religiously devoted.

• Option 3: Layperson (साधारण व्यक्ति): A person who is not ordained or professionally trained in a particular field (especially religion) — the opposite of someone formally dedicated to religious life.

• Option 4: Secular (धर्मनिरपेक्ष): Relating to worldly, non-religious matters — directly opposite to the religious sense of "oblate".

NOTE

• "Oblate" also has an unrelated geometry sense: a sphere flattened at the poles (e.g., "the Earth is an oblate spheroid") — SSC vocabulary questions typically test the religious-noun sense.

• Related religious-life vocabulary: novice (one in training before taking full vows), cleric (an ordained religious official), ascetic (one who practices strict self-discipline for religious reasons).

• The blank follows "more than 60" and precedes "of rat", and the next clause explains "which means they come in all sizes" — this refers to different biological classifications/types of rats, which is precisely what "species" means in a taxonomic context.

• Rule — Contextual word choice in cloze passages: Always read the sentence(s) immediately before and after the blank, since the passage often explains or hints at the missing word (here, the taxonomic reference "Integrated Taxonomic Information System" and the following clause about "all sizes" both point to "species").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "entities" is too vague and generic; it does not fit the specific taxonomic/biological context of classifying types of rats.

• Option 2: "sections" refers to divisions or parts of something else (like a document or an organisation), not to biological classification.

• Option 4: "objects" is incorrect because rats are living creatures being classified biologically, not "objects".

NOTE

• "Species" is the basic unit of biological classification, below "genus" — commonly tested vocabulary in science-based comprehension passages.

• In cloze passages, always check whether the missing word must agree grammatically and logically with surrounding technical terms (here, "Taxonomic Information System" is a strong clue toward "species").

solution_text:

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states the Bosavi woolly rat "was ______ in 2009 in the rainforest of Papua New Guinea (and doesn't have a scientific name yet)" — since it is a naturally occurring animal that scientists came upon for the first time, the correct verb is "discovered", not "invented" (which applies to creating something new that did not exist before).

• Rule — Contextual word choice in cloze passages: For naturally existing things (animals, places, phenomena) that are found for the first time, use "discover"; for man-made objects or ideas created for the first time, use "invent".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "invented" is incorrect because a living species is not created/invented by humans; it already exists in nature and is only found/identified.

• Option 3: "denuded" means stripped bare or made naked, which does not logically fit the context of a species being found.

• Option 4: "screened" means examined or filtered for a particular purpose, which does not fit the sense of a first-time finding of a new species.

NOTE

• Classic SSC pair: "discover" (find something that already existed but was previously unknown) vs "invent" (create something new that did not exist before) — e.g., Columbus discovered America; Edison invented the light bulb.

• The clue "(and doesn't have a scientific name yet)" strongly supports "discovered", since newly discovered species are formally named only after scientific study.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads "It is ______ the size of a cat", giving an approximate comparison of size. The word that expresses approximation before a noun phrase like "the size of" is "about" (meaning "approximately").

• Rule — Contextual word choice in cloze passages: "About" functions here as an adverb of approximation modifying the noun phrase "the size of a cat", a standard construction ("about the size of...", "about as big as...").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a lot" is used to express a large quantity or degree (e.g., "a lot bigger than"), not to introduce an approximate size comparison in this structure.

• Option 2: "of" is a preposition that cannot grammatically begin this phrase; it does not express approximation.

• Option 4: "some" is used before plural or uncountable nouns to mean "a certain amount/number of", and does not fit the singular comparative structure "the size of a cat".

NOTE

• Common approximation words tested by SSC: about, approximately, roughly, nearly, around — all can express "close to" a stated figure or comparison.

• The fixed expression "about the size of" is a common construction used to describe dimensions informally, especially in journalistic writing (as seen here, quoting CNN).

• Rule — Contextual word choice in cloze passages: The verb must agree with the unit that follows it: units of length (inches, cm) pair with "measures", while units of mass (lbs., kilograms) pair with "weighs".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "evaluates" means to assess or judge the value/quality of something, which does not fit stating a numerical weight.

• Option 3: "counts" means to determine a number of discrete items, which does not fit describing weight in pounds/kilograms.

• Option 4: "measures" would logically pair with units of length (like the "32.2 inches" mentioned earlier in the same sentence), not with units of mass like "lbs." and "kilograms".

NOTE

• Remember the distinction: "measures" is typically used with length/height/dimension units (inches, cm, metres), while "weighs" is used with mass units (kg, lbs., grams) — a frequent SSC cloze-passage trap.

• The same sentence tests both concepts together: "...32.2 inches (82 cm) from nose to tail [measures – length] and weighs around 3.3 lbs. (1.5 kilograms) [weight] according to CNN."
